planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this Sichuan endemic is grown for its unusual spurless, hanging bell-shaped flowers rather than the long-spurred blooms typical of most epimedium.

directions: Epimedium campanulatum was found in the mountains of northwestern Sichuan and stands apart from most of its relatives by lacking petal spurs entirely, instead producing four soft yellow petals that hang together as a small dangling bell. A single stem can carry a remarkably dense inflorescence of fifteen to forty of these bells in an upright pyramidal spray held above compact, wiry rhizomes and paired trifoliolate leaves. Because it comes from a narrow native range at elevation, give it a cool, sheltered position with reliably moist, humus-rich soil rather than the drier shade tolerated by tougher garden epimedium. It increases slowly, so plan on leaving clumps undisturbed for several years before dividing.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; broad-petalled epimedium is a narrowly distributed Chinese species with short, spreading rhizomes and small, spurless yellow flowers.

directions: Epimedium platypetalum is a semi-evergreen species from Sichuan and southwestern Shanxi that stays low and compact, each thin rhizome sending up a single trifoliolate leaf and a short flowering stem. Its small, spurless flowers are pale yellow and bell-like, borne only a few to a stem, giving the plant a much daintier presence than the showier long-spurred hybrids common in gardens. It suits the front of a shaded rock garden or a trough where its fine scale and creeping habit can be appreciated up close. Keep the soil evenly moist and humus-rich, since this species has a narrow native range and does not tolerate prolonged drought as readily as more widespread garden epimedium.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Epstein's epimedium was collected in Hunan province and is valued as a vigorous, large-flowered groundcover for woodland plantings.

directions: Epimedium epsteinii was collected in Hunan in the 1990s and named for plantsman Harold Epstein; it stands out for having the widest sepals of any species in the genus, pure white and forming a striking backdrop to the reddish-purple spurs and cup of each medium-large flower. A single stem can hold ten to thirty of these blooms, making established clumps unusually showy in mid-spring compared to the more modest flower counts of many other Epimedium species. It builds into an effective, weed-suppressing groundcover at a faster pace than many Chinese epimedium and works well massed along a woodland path or beneath deciduous shrubs. Plant it in consistently moist, humus-rich soil, and divide congested clumps in late summer or fall once flowering has finished.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade sheltered from cold, drying winds; few-flowered epimedium is a diminutive Sichuan species whose evergreen leaves emerge bronze-mottled before turning glossy green.

directions: Epimedium pauciflorum is one of the smaller evergreen species, forming a tidy clump under eight inches tall of sharply toothed, heart-shaped leaflets that open mottled with bronze in spring before settling into glossy green. Its sparse sprays of small flowers pair white sepals with spurred petals that range from white to pale pink, a color variability documented in wild Sichuan populations of the species. Because the foliage is evergreen and the plant is compact, it makes a good choice for the front edge of a shaded bed or a woodland rock garden where winter structure matters. Give it shelter from harsh winter wind and consistently moist, well-drained soil to keep the foliage from browning.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; broad-sepaled epimedium is a Sichuan species prized for unusually large, nodding white flowers held above narrow evergreen foliage.

directions: Epimedium latisepalum takes its name from its unusually broad inner sepals, which spread horizontally beneath large creamy white flowers touched with purple at the base of each petal and finished with slender, slightly arching white spurs. Loose, few-flowered sprays open in mid-spring on wiry stems that rise well above a low clump of narrow, evergreen leaflets, giving the two-inch blooms room to nod and display fully. Its outsized flower size relative to a fairly compact plant makes it a good specimen near a path edge or bench where the blooms can be viewed up close. Grow it as with other Sichuan epimedium species, in reliably moist, humus-rich soil, and avoid letting the site dry out during the growing season.
